title: AI use, personal control, and confidence in public or private AI are separate country-level surfaces
source_unit: 2025 UNDP Global Survey on AI and Human Development respondent; country-weighted descriptive comparison
geography: United States and selected comparison countries from a 21-country survey

denominator.unit: US survey respondents; weighted denominator varies by item

used_ai_at_least_weekly.unit: percent; Q10 once a week or more than once a week

confident_control_ai_interactions.unit: percent; Q16 agree or strongly agree

confident_government_can_use_ai.unit: percent; Q18 very or somewhat confident

confident_ai_designed_in_people_interest.unit: percent; Q19 very or somewhat confident

observations.method: Weighted descriptive tabulation of the UNDP 2025 Global Survey on AI and Human Development Stata file using Weight_none_resp1; special response codes and item nonresponse excluded from each item denominator.
observations.uncertainty: The file is a cross-sectional survey with country samples of roughly 1,000, not a panel or representative estimate of all US residents. Items have different valid universes; no complex-design standard errors were calculated in this pass. Country comparisons may reflect sampling, translation, institutional context, question interpretation, and weighting differences.
observations.subgroup: US respondents; no age, gender, education, work, income, or place stratification in this first pass.
observations.counterinterpretation: Low confidence can coexist with frequent use, and high confidence can reflect general optimism or institutional trust rather than effective control. The measures do not establish productivity, harm, or actual public-service quality.

denominator.unit: China survey respondents; weighted denominator varies by item

used_ai_at_least_weekly.unit: percent; Q10 once a week or more than once a week

confident_control_ai_interactions.unit: percent; Q16 agree or strongly agree

confident_government_can_use_ai.unit: percent; Q18 very or somewhat confident

confident_ai_designed_in_people_interest.unit: percent; Q19 very or somewhat confident

observations.method: Same weighted descriptive tabulation and item coding as the US observation.
observations.uncertainty: Cross-country differences are descriptive and may include survey-mode, translation, institutional, political, and cultural response differences. They do not identify a country effect or establish that public confidence corresponds to actual AI governance.
observations.subgroup: China respondents; no subgroup stratification in this pass.
observations.counterinterpretation: High confidence in government or AI design may reflect trust, expectations, or response style rather than observed service quality or personal control.

denominator.unit: Germany survey respondents; weighted denominator varies by item

used_ai_at_least_weekly.unit: percent; Q10 once a week or more than once a week

confident_control_ai_interactions.unit: percent; Q16 agree or strongly agree

confident_government_can_use_ai.unit: percent; Q18 very or somewhat confident

confident_ai_designed_in_people_interest.unit: percent; Q19 very or somewhat confident

observations.method: Same weighted descriptive tabulation and item coding as the US observation.
observations.uncertainty: This is a country comparison, not a causal comparison. The measures have different item missingness and do not capture workplace rules, privacy law, service performance, or actual control.
observations.subgroup: Germany respondents; no subgroup stratification in this pass.
observations.counterinterpretation: More frequent use can coexist with less reported personal control; that relationship may reflect task exposure, skepticism, or different interpretations of control.

denominator.unit: South Africa survey respondents; weighted denominator varies by item

used_ai_at_least_weekly.unit: percent; Q10 once a week or more than once a week

confident_control_ai_interactions.unit: percent; Q16 agree or strongly agree

confident_government_can_use_ai.unit: percent; Q18 very or somewhat confident

confident_ai_designed_in_people_interest.unit: percent; Q19 very or somewhat confident

observations.method: Same weighted descriptive tabulation and item coding as the US observation.
observations.uncertainty: Country estimates are descriptive, and the comparison does not harmonize labor-market composition, internet access, survey mode, or institutional context. No inference about development, governance quality, or AI outcomes follows from these percentages.
observations.subgroup: South Africa respondents; no subgroup stratification in this pass.
observations.counterinterpretation: High reported use may indicate greater exposure or different access, not greater benefit; confidence in AI may reflect expectations rather than realized agency.

observations.period: 2025; United States subgroup comparison by age

denominator.unit: US respondents; age-group cells: 15–17 n=55, 18–35 n=243, 36–59 n=367, 60+ n=340

weekly_use_by_age.unit: weighted percent; Q10 once a week or more

control_confidence_by_age.unit: weighted percent; Q16 agree or strongly agree

government_confidence_by_age.unit: weighted percent; Q18 very or somewhat confident

design_confidence_by_age.unit: weighted percent; Q19 very or somewhat confident

observations.method: Same weighted descriptive tabulation as the country comparison, stratified by UNDP survey AgeGroup; item nonresponse and special codes excluded separately.
observations.uncertainty: The 15–17 cell is small, no complex-design standard errors were calculated, and age is associated with education, employment, access, and survey interpretation. These are descriptive subgroup differences, not age effects.
observations.counterinterpretation: Lower reported use among older respondents may reflect access, purpose, exposure, or cohort differences rather than lower ability or lower benefit. Higher confidence among younger respondents does not establish greater control.

observations.period: 2025; United States subgroup comparison by gender

denominator.unit: US respondents; gender cells: female n=495, male n=497, other n=13

weekly_use_by_gender.unit: weighted percent; Q10 once a week or more

control_confidence_by_gender.unit: weighted percent; Q16 agree or strongly agree

government_confidence_by_gender.unit: weighted percent; Q18 very or somewhat confident

design_confidence_by_gender.unit: weighted percent; Q19 very or somewhat confident

observations.method: Same weighted descriptive tabulation as the country comparison, stratified by Q2 gender; item nonresponse and special codes excluded separately.
observations.uncertainty: The Other cell has only 13 respondents and is not stable for interpretation; no complex-design standard errors were calculated. Gender categories are survey response categories, not a complete account of identity or mechanism.
observations.subgroup: US respondents by reported gender: female, male, and other.
observations.counterinterpretation: Differences may reflect age, work, education, access, task purpose, or exposure rather than gender itself; the very small Other cell should not be compared as a precise estimate.

observations.period: 2025; United States subgroup comparison by education

denominator.unit: US respondents with valid mapped education; cells: primary or less n=143, some secondary n=70, secondary completed n=396, university+ n=388

weekly_use_by_education.value: Primary or less: 31.2%; Some secondary: 44.0%; Secondary completed: 29.9%; University+: 36.2%
weekly_use_by_education.unit: weighted percent; Q10 once a week or more

control_confidence_by_education.value: Primary or less: 38.2%; Some secondary: 43.2%; Secondary completed: 36.8%; University+: 46.3%
control_confidence_by_education.unit: weighted percent; Q16 agree or strongly agree

government_confidence_by_education.value: Primary or less: 23.0%; Some secondary: 31.3%; Secondary completed: 27.6%; University+: 32.5%
government_confidence_by_education.unit: weighted percent; Q18 very or somewhat confident

design_confidence_by_education.value: Primary or less: 32.1%; Some secondary: 40.9%; Secondary completed: 39.3%; University+: 34.3%
design_confidence_by_education.unit: weighted percent; Q19 very or somewhat confident

observations.method: Same weighted descriptive tabulation as the country comparison, stratified by Q3mapped education; invalid, don’t-know, and prefer-not-to-answer codes excluded.
observations.uncertainty: The education cells are not equally sized, no complex-design standard errors were calculated, and education is entangled with age, employment, income, internet access, and task exposure. These are descriptive differences, not education effects.
observations.subgroup: US respondents by mapped education: primary or less, some secondary, secondary completed, and university or more.
observations.counterinterpretation: Education is not monotonic in every measure: university respondents report more personal-control confidence but not the highest design confidence or weekly use. This cautions against treating credentials as a complete proxy for AI agency.

observations.period: 2025; United States same-survey AI-use frequency by perceived control

denominator.unit: US respondents with valid AI-use and control responses; weekly-or-more n=301, monthly-or-less n=650

control_confidence_weekly_or_more.unit: weighted percent; Q10 weekly-or-more users who agree or strongly agree they can control AI interactions

control_confidence_monthly_or_less.unit: weighted percent; Q10 monthly-or-less users who agree or strongly agree

observations.method: Weighted descriptive cross-tabulation of Q10 AI-use frequency and Q16 perceived ability to control AI interactions using Weight_none_resp1; don’t-know and prefer-not-to-answer codes excluded.
observations.uncertainty: The two measures are simultaneous self-reports, so the contrast cannot establish that use increases control. People with more control may choose to use AI more, or age, education, work, access, and purpose may shape both responses. No complex-design standard errors were calculated.
observations.subgroup: US respondents grouped as weekly-or-more versus monthly-or-less AI users; once-a-week and more-than-once-a-week are combined for the first group.
observations.counterinterpretation: Frequent users may be more knowledgeable, more exposed, or more confident in reporting—not necessarily more protected. Infrequent users may have less opportunity to learn control or may avoid systems they distrust.

observations.period: 2025; United States same-survey AI-use frequency by institutional confidence

denominator.unit: US respondents with valid AI-use and item responses; weekly-or-more and monthly-or-less cells vary by item

government_confidence_weekly_or_more.unit: weighted percent; weekly-or-more users very or somewhat confident government can use AI

government_confidence_monthly_or_less.unit: weighted percent; monthly-or-less users very or somewhat confident

design_confidence_weekly_or_more.unit: weighted percent; weekly-or-more users very or somewhat confident AI is designed in people’s interests

design_confidence_monthly_or_less.unit: weighted percent; monthly-or-less users very or somewhat confident

observations.method: Weighted descriptive cross-tabulation of Q10 AI-use frequency with Q18 government confidence and Q19 design confidence using Weight_none_resp1; item-specific valid universes retained.
observations.uncertainty: The cross-tab is associative and simultaneous, with item-specific missingness and no complex-design standard errors. It does not show that use causes confidence or that confidence reflects actual quality, fairness, or control.
observations.subgroup: US respondents grouped as weekly-or-more versus monthly-or-less AI users.
observations.counterinterpretation: People who use AI more may have jobs, education, or access that also make institutions seem more familiar or useful. Confidence could precede use rather than follow it.

observations.period: 2025; United States reported AI use by life domain

denominator.unit: US survey respondents; Q11 domain-use items

used_ai_for_financial_services.unit: percent answering yes for financial services or banking

used_ai_for_healthcare.unit: percent answering yes for healthcare services or applications

used_ai_for_work_tools.unit: percent answering yes for work-related tools or software

used_ai_for_education.unit: percent answering yes for educational platforms or learning apps

used_ai_for_government_services.unit: percent answering yes for government services such as taxes or judicial services

observations.method: Weighted descriptive tabulation of the UNDP Q11 yes/no domain-use items using Weight_none_resp1; each item is treated as a separate response and is not interpreted as exclusive.
observations.uncertainty: The items do not establish frequency, purpose depth, quality, or whether the respondent directly interacted with an AI system. Domain items can overlap and the survey wording includes broad examples; no complex-design standard errors were calculated.
observations.subgroup: US respondents; no age, gender, education, work, or income stratification in this observation.
observations.counterinterpretation: A reported domain use can be incidental or mediated by a platform and does not prove reliance, benefit, harm, or loss of human choice. Low reported government-service use does not mean low exposure to automated public systems.

denominator.unit: US survey respondents; valid Q12 item denominators vary from 957 to 966

likely_use_for_entertainment.unit: percent somewhat or very likely; valid n=966

likely_use_for_education.unit: percent somewhat or very likely; valid n=964

likely_use_for_work.unit: percent somewhat or very likely; valid n=961

likely_use_for_medical_advice.unit: percent somewhat or very likely; valid n=961

likely_use_for_financial_advice.unit: percent somewhat or very likely; valid n=957

observations.method: Weighted descriptive tabulation of Q12 likelihood-of-use items using Weight_none_resp1; somewhat likely and very likely combined, with item-specific valid denominators.
observations.uncertainty: Likelihood is an intention or expectation, not observed use. The items are not a forecast and may be influenced by perceived usefulness, social desirability, trust, access, or question order. No complex-design standard errors were calculated.
observations.subgroup: US respondents; no subgroup stratification in this observation.
observations.counterinterpretation: High expected use for entertainment or education does not imply high stakes or high dependence; lower expected use for finance does not imply low financial exposure to automated systems.

denominator.unit: US survey respondents; Q21 expectation items

expect_productivity_increase.unit: percent likely or very likely AI will increase productivity at work

expect_new_job_roles.unit: percent likely or very likely AI will help find new job roles

expect_current_job_changed_or_replaced.unit: percent likely or very likely current job will be significantly changed or replaced

observations.method: Weighted descriptive tabulation of Q21 work-expectation items using Weight_none_resp1; likely and very likely combined.
observations.uncertainty: These are expectations, not observed productivity, job creation, displacement, or wage outcomes. The survey does not restrict the items to currently employed respondents in this record; no complex-design standard errors were calculated.
observations.subgroup: US respondents; no employment, occupation, age, education, or income stratification in this observation.
observations.counterinterpretation: People can expect productivity gains and job disruption simultaneously; expectations may reflect public narratives, sector exposure, or uncertainty rather than a forecast of the respondent’s own job.

observations.period: 2025; United States expected productivity by likely work use

denominator.unit: US respondents with valid Q12 work-use and Q21 productivity responses; likely-work-use n=456, unlikely-work-use n=505

productivity_expectation_likely_work_use.unit: weighted percent likely or very likely productivity increases among Q12 somewhat/very likely work-use group

productivity_expectation_unlikely_work_u.unit: weighted percent likely or very likely productivity increases among Q12 not-at-all/not-very-likely work-use group

observations.method: Weighted descriptive cross-tabulation of Q12 likelihood of AI use for work tasks and Q21 expected productivity increase using Weight_none_resp1; neutral, don’t-know, and prefer-not-to-answer codes excluded.
observations.uncertainty: The measures are simultaneous expectations and cannot establish that expected use causes expected productivity. The contrast may reflect occupation, education, access, optimism, or selection into work-related AI use; no complex-design standard errors were calculated.
observations.subgroup: US respondents divided by likely versus unlikely future AI use for work tasks.
observations.counterinterpretation: Confidence in productivity may lead people to expect use, rather than result from it. Neither expectation identifies who receives the gain, whose work changes, or whether worker voice rises.

related_sources.claim: UNDP metadata workbook documents the survey fields and supports reproducible variable interpretation.
The questionnaire supplies the wording and response scales for use, control, trust, and AI-purpose measures.

boundary: This is a weighted descriptive comparison from the UNDP 2025 Global Survey on AI and Human Development. It establishes that AI use, perceived personal control, confidence in government use, and confidence in AI design vary separately across selected countries, not that any country causes those differences or that confidence equals actual control, benefit, service quality, worker power, or human development. The survey is cross-sectional and the raw Stata file is captured by hash but not committed to the repository.
